The `tunnelRoute` option makes the SDK send browser events to a path on your own Next.js server (for example `/monitoring`), where a rewrite forwards them to Sentry to prevent ad blockers from blocking them. To keep those envelope requests from being rejected by your middleware, the SDK skips middleware for them.

The middleware skip was wider than the rewrite. The rewrite only serves requests to the tunnel path itself with the `o` and `p` parameters set. The skip applied to anything under the tunnel path. Requests in that gap go to your application instead of Sentry, and your middleware never runs on them.

Skipping middleware does not grant the request any privileges. Routes that check the session server-side are still protected.

You are affected only if **all** of the following are true:

1. `tunnelRoute` is set (a string path or `true`),
2. your app is built with **webpack** (Turbopack builds are not affected),
3. some route of your application resolves under the tunnel path. That could be a direct collision (`/monitoring/foo` with `tunnelRoute: '/monitoring'`) or a dynamic segment at the route root (`app/[locale]/…`), which matches any first path segment, and

`useHeadSafe` restricts head input to an allowlist of safe tags and attributes. For example, `bodyAttrs` is limited to `class` and `style`, event handler attributes are removed, and `<script>` tags are only kept for JSON types.

When `useHeadSafe` is called inside a server island (a `.server.vue` component or page, or a component rendered with `<NuxtIsland>`), the island renderer serialises the raw input of every head entry into the island response without the option that marks it as safe input. `<NuxtIsland>` then pushes that input into the page's head as a regular entry, both during server rendering and when hydrating or refetching on the client.

As a result, input that `useHeadSafe` would normally strip (such as `bodyAttrs.onload` or executable `<script>` content) is rendered into the page. If an application passes user-controlled data to `useHeadSafe` inside a server island, an attacker who controls that data can achieve stored cross-site scripting on the application's origin.

// author.value.head is user-authored, e.g. { bodyAttrs: { onl

## Impact

With the default `router.options.sensitive: false`, Nuxt's page router resolves routes case-insensitively, so `/Admin` renders the same page as `/admin`. On the server, however, route rules were resolved with Nitro's route-rule matcher, which matches keys case-sensitively. A request whose path differs from a rule key only in letter case therefore rendered the page with none of that rule applied.

Earlier fixes ([GHSA-mm7m-92g8-7m47](https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/security/advisories/GHSA-mm7m-92g8-7m47), [GHSA-hxvh-4h3w-prp9](https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/security/advisories/GHSA-hxvh-4h3w-prp9)) case-folded the route rules that the Nuxt app itself reads, such as `appMiddleware`. This advisory covers the rules applied on the server:

- `redirect`: a rule used to send visitors away from a page, such as `'/admin/**': { redirect: '/login' }`, was skipped, and the page and its server-fetched data were rendered instead.
- `headers`: per-route response headers, including security headers such as `Content-Security-Policy` or `X-Frame-Options`, were not sent.
- `proxy`: the request was not proxied.
- `ssr: false` and `noScripts`: the page was server-rendered, or shipped scripts, de

### Summary

Nuxt compared `routeRules` keys against the raw request path, without decoding percent-encoding, while the router decodes parameters when it resolves a route. A request whose path is percent-encoded can therefore resolve to a page while failing to match the route rule meant to protect it, so the rule's `appMiddleware` never runs, including during server rendering.

### Impact

For a page served through a dynamic or catch-all route, an attacker can percent-encode a character in the path to skip the rule:

```ts
export default defineNuxtConfig({
  routeRules: {
    '/users/admin': { appMiddleware: 'auth' },
  },
})
```

Requesting `/users/%61dmin` still renders `app/pages/users/[id].vue` with `id` decoded to `admin`, but the rule keyed `/users/admin` does not match, so `auth` does not run and the server renders and returns the gated page to an unauthenticated visitor. No privileges and no user interaction are required, and only ASCII characters are involved.

Purely static ASCII routes are not affected: static segments are matched without decoding, so a request for `/%61dmin` does not resolve to the page registered at `/admin` and 404s instead of rendering.

## Impact

An application that renders `<NuxtLink :to="...">` with a value it does not control can be made to render an anchor whose `href` executes script in the application's origin when clicked.

This is an incomplete fix for [GHSA-934w-87qh-qr26](https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/security/advisories/GHSA-934w-87qh-qr26) (CVE-2026-53722). It only affects applications running without a `pages/` directory, where `pages` resolves to `false` and Nuxt registers its own router in place of vue-router. Applications using vue-router are not affected.

Prefixing `javascript:` with an ASCII C0 control character, for example `%01`, meant the value was not recognised as having a protocol. It was classified as an internal route and so never reached the protocol check added in GHSA-934w-87qh-qr26, and the router used for `pages: false` passed it through to the rendered `href` unchanged. Browsers strip the leading control character and run the result as a script URL.

Both `<NuxtLink custom>` and the default anchor are affected, and the `href` is present in the server-rendered HTML.

`FlexAssembler`, the custom-container assembler shipped in the `stream-json` package (`src/core/utils/flex-assembler.js`, re-exported at `stream-json/utils/flex-assembler.js` and `stream-json/web/utils/flex-assembler.js`), compiles a string or RegExp path `filter` into a matcher that runs `keyStack.join(separator)` on every container start. Because the key stack grows one entry per open object or array with no depth bound, a JSON document nested to depth D drives D container-start tokens that each perform an O(D) join, for O(D^2) total CPU on the single-threaded event loop. An unauthenticated party who can supply JSON bytes to a pipeline that uses a `FlexAssembler` with a string or RegExp rule filter can stall the process with a small input: roughly 96 KB (depth 16000) blocks the event loop for over a second, and the cost grows quadratically.

## Root Cause

`FlexAssembler` reconstructs JavaScript values from the parser token stream and supports custom containers selected by path-matching rules. ## Summary

Astro's JSX and MDX rendering pipeline treated string children of `<script>` and `<style>` elements as trusted HTML. When a dynamic value was passed through a JSX expression, such as `<script>{value}</script>`, an attacker-controlled value containing `</script>` or `</style>` could terminate the element and inject arbitrary HTML and JavaScript.

Other JSX expression contexts escaped dynamic strings automatically. This behavior was limited to `<script>` and `<style>` children rendered through Astro's `astro:jsx` renderer, including MDX components.

## Details

The affected rendering paths marked all string children of `<script>` and `<style>` elements as safe HTML, without distinguishing literal content generated by the compiler from dynamic expression values. An application was vulnerable when attacker-controlled data, such as a query parameter or CMS field, was interpolated directly into one of these elements.

For example, a value containing `</script><script>alert(1)</script>` passed to `<script>{value}</script>` was emitted without escaping. The browser interpreted the first closing tag as markup and executed the injected script.

### Summary

Astro's server-side View Transition CSS generator did not keep string animation properties within their generated CSS declarations. In an application that passes attacker-controlled data into an animation property such as `duration`, a value containing CSS delimiters could terminate the declaration and rule, then add attacker-selected CSS to the server-rendered page.

The injected content remains inside the generated `<style>` element. It cannot terminate that element or inject HTML or JavaScript because Astro escapes `<` before emitting the stylesheet.

### Severity

Exploitation requires an application to pass untrusted, request-derived, or user-controlled content directly into a transition animation value. This is an uncommon application pattern, and applications using static or otherwise trusted transition values are unaffected.

The resulting capability is limited to CSS in the rendered document. The proof of concept does not demonstrate JavaScript execution, HTML injection, an origin-boundary bypass, or access to server-only data.

**Summary:** The Storybook dev server exposes its WebSocket authentication token to any client that can load its HTML pages. Any host on a LAN can open a Storybook app by IP address, and therefore obtain the token. The WebSocket can be used to inject code into story files or to create new files. Under the right circumstances, an attacker can execute code on the machine of a developer connected on the same LAN.

## Who is impacted?

You are impacted if you run a Storybook dev server whilst connected on an untrusted local network, or to a WiFi access point posing as a trusted network. The impact of this advisory is more important if you have the Vitest addon installed and are using an old version of Vitest.

You are not impacted if:

- You run a dev server in an environment that other devices on your network cannot reach (e.g. a container that does not publish the Storybook port, or publishes it only on `127.0.0.1`)
- You run a dev server whilst connected to a trusted local network
- You serve a built version of Storybook on your machine

### Impact
In offscreen rendering mode on macOS, frame data received from the GPU process was not fully validated by the main process. A compromised GPU process could cause the main process to read out-of-bounds memory while producing `paint` event images, disclosing memory or crashing the app. GHSA-pfmc-3mgc-p6fp covers the same issue on the other capture paths.

Apps are only affected if they use offscreen rendering (`webPreferences.offscreen`) on macOS and an attacker has separately gained code execution in the GPU process. Apps that do not use offscreen rendering are not affected.

### Workarounds
There are no app side workarounds, you must update to a patched version of Electron.

### Fixed Versions

* `44.4.3`
* `43.7.3`
* `42.11.6`

### For more information
If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, email us at [security@electronjs.org](mailto:security@electronjs.org)

Apps are only affected if they use `webContents.beginFrameSubscription` and an attacker has separately gained code execution in the GPU process. Apps that do not subscribe to captured frames are not affected.

### Impact
Requests to open external protocol URLs could be attributed to a document other than the one that asked for them, so the `requestingUrl` passed to `session.setPermissionRequestHandler` was a trusted origin for a launch untrusted content had requested. An origin-based handler could therefore let untrusted content launch an OS-registered external application.

Apps are only affected if they grant `openExternal` based on the requesting origin and let untrusted content open or navigate windows. Apps whose permission handler denies `openExternal` for untrusted content are not affected.

### Workarounds
Deny the `openExternal` permission for untrusted content, or deny the windows it opens with `setWindowOpenHandler`.

### Impact
For `pointerLock` permission requests made from some cross-origin iframes, `session.setPermissionRequestHandler()` was given the top-level frame's `requestingUrl` and `isMainFrame` instead of the requesting frame's. Apps that grant pointer lock based on the requesting origin could grant it to embedded content under the top-level page's identity.

Apps are only affected if they embed untrusted content in iframes and decide `pointerLock` requests by origin in `setPermissionRequestHandler`. Apps that do not embed untrusted content, or that deny `pointerLock` for it, are not affected.

### Workarounds
Deny the `pointerLock` permission for web contents that embed untrusted frames.

### Fixed Versions
* `45.0.0-alpha.13`
* `44.5.0`
* `43.7.6`
* `42.11.9`

### For more information
If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, email us at [security@electronjs.org](mailto:security@electronjs.org)

### Impact
`chrome.tabs.query()` returned each tab's `url` and `title` to extensions that held neither the `tabs` permission nor matching host permissions, so any loaded extension could read the URL and title of every webContents in its session.

Apps are only affected if they load extensions (`session.extensions.loadExtension`) that they do not fully trust. Apps that load no extensions, or only trusted ones, are not affected.

### Workarounds
Do not load untrusted or unvalidated extensions. In general you should only load trusted extensions.

### Fixed Versions
* `45.0.0-alpha.4`
* `44.1.1`
* `43.5.1`
* `42.11.1`

### For more information

### Impact

Pages opened into a new window from a link were loaded as if the app itself had navigated there rather than the page that contained the link, so the request was treated as same-site: `SameSite=Strict` cookies were sent and `Sec-Fetch-Site` did not identify the initiating page. Content shown in the app could use this to make a credentialed top-level request to another site that relies on SameSite cookies as a CSRF defence.

Apps are only affected if they load untrusted content and allow it to open new windows. Apps that deny new windows from untrusted content with `setWindowOpenHandler` are not affected.

### Workarounds

Return `{ action: 'deny' }` from `setWindowOpenHandler` for windows opened by untrusted content.

### Fixed Versions

When nodemailer DKIM-signs an outbound message, its DKIM message parser unfolds RFC 5322 header continuation lines with a loop that concatenates each continuation line onto the preceding line and then re-tests the anchored regex `/^[ \t]/` against the growing merged line on every iteration. Re-testing the regex against the ever-growing accumulated line forces a full string flatten proportional to the accumulated length on each iteration, yielding O(n^2) CPU in the number of continuation lines. An application user who influences the size of a header that folds into many continuation lines (most naturally a large recipient list, but also a long custom header, Subject, or References) can drive tens of thousands of continuation lines and block the single-threaded Node.js event loop for seconds during signing, a repeatable denial of service.

The invariant that signing a message performs work linear in the message size is violated in the header-unfolding step. ### Impact

Fastify lowercases header names in a `headers` schema before compilation, because Node.js stores request header names in lowercase. This normalization does not reach the header names held in a `propertyNames` subschema's `enum` and `const`. A header-name deny-list written in the canonical header case, such as `propertyNames: { not: { enum: ['X-Debug-Override'] } }`, therefore never matches the lowercased request headers, and the forbidden header reaches the handler. Any application that uses a `propertyNames` deny-list or allow-list to constrain request header names does not get the constraint it expects. The same rule written in lowercase works, and the `not: { required: [...] }` form is unaffected, so this is a gap in the built-in normalization rather than a wrong schema. This is an incomplete fix of CVE-2026-84428 ([GHSA-9q9j-q6p8-xq58](https://github.com/fastify/fastify/security/advisories/GHSA-9q9j-q6p8-xq58)), whose normalization covered header names used as property keys but not those used as values inside `propertyNames`.

### Patches

Users should upgrade to fastify `5.12.6` or later, which lowercases header names held in `enum` and `const` inside a `propertyNa

vulnerabilities.description:
### Impact

With Cache Components enabled (`cacheComponents: true`), a `'use cache'` function that calls another `'use cache'` function that reads a root param can be keyed incorrectly when the inner call is served from an existing entry: the enclosing function's cache key then omits that root param. The enclosing entry is written once and reused for all root param values, so a response for one root param value can serve content produced for a different value — whether the page is prerendered at build time or at runtime, or rendered dynamically. Shared cache headers let downstream caches redistribute the content further. 

What values are leaked cannot be attacker controlled. Which value's content is served depends only on which invocation wrote the entry first.

### Workarounds

There are no known workarounds. Apps should upgrade to the patched version as soon as possible.

### Summary

Browser CDP discovery could accept blocked WebSocket URLs. In affected versions, a lower-trust caller or configured input path could reach network destinations that should have been blocked by OpenClaw policy.

This advisory is scoped to the named feature and configuration. It does not change OpenClaw's trusted-operator model: authenticated Gateway operators, installed plugins, and intentional local execution surfaces remain trusted unless a separate policy, approval, allowlist, sandbox, or auth boundary is crossed.

### Impact

When the affected feature is enabled and reachable, this could reach network destinations that should have been blocked by OpenClaw policy. Practical impact depends on the operator's configuration and whether lower-trust input can reach that path.

### Patched Versions

The first stable patched version is `2026.6.6`.

### Mitigations

Upgrade to a patched OpenClaw release when one is listed. Before upgrading, restrict the affected feature to trusted operators or disable it when it is not needed. As general hardening, keep channel and tool allowlists narrow, avoid sharing one Gateway between mutually untrusted users, and disable the affected fea

**Summary:** A malicious website may be able to cause unauthorized file changes in a developer’s project while an affected Storybook development server is running. Under additional conditions, a changed file could be executed by a local runtime with the developer’s privileges. We are not aware of exploitation in the wild.

## Who is impacted?

You are impacted if you run a Storybook dev server in the affected versions.

You are not impacted if:

- You run a dev server that you never open in a web browser (e.g. headless automation, MCP clients)
- You run or visit a built version of Storybook

Recent versions of Chrome and Firefox may ask for permission before a website can connect to a `localhost` service. This reduces the risk, but does not remove it. Do not grant this permission to websites you don’t trust.

## Recommended actions

### Upgrade Storybook

Storybook has released patched versions of all affected major Storybook versions that fix all the vulnerabilities necessary for the worst-case scenario above to occur. 

Upgrade to a patched version listed below before running `storybook dev` again. If you cannot upgrade immediately, do not run an affected Storybook dev server unt

### Impact
For `hid` and `usb` permission checks made from an iframe, `session.setPermissionCheckHandler` was given the top-level frame's origin and details instead of the requesting frame's. Apps that allow these permissions based on origin could grant an embedded frame access intended for the top-level page.

You're only affected if you use `setPermissionCheckHandler` with origin-based logic for `hid` or `usb` and embed cross-origin iframes with `allow="hid"` or `allow="usb"`. Apps that don't delegate those features to untrusted iframes are not affected.

### Workarounds
Don't add `allow="hid"` / `allow="usb"` to untrusted iframes, or make the decision in your `select-hid-device` / `select-usb-device` handler using `details.frame`.

### Fixed Versions
* `45.0.0-alpha.5`
* `44.3.0`
* `43.7.0`
* `42.11.3`

### For more information
If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, email us at [security@electronjs.org](mailto:security@electronjs.org)

## Summary

A potential unauthenticated denial-of-service vulnerability exists in the chunked import upload path used by `@apostrophecms/import-export`.

The affected import API routes invoke:

`self.apos.http.bigUploadMiddleware()`

before the actual import handler performs its authentication check.

Because no `authorize` callback is supplied to `bigUploadMiddleware()`, unauthenticated requests can reach the `aposBigUpload` `start`, `chunk`, and `end` operations before the later `req.user` check rejects the import.

As a result, an unauthenticated remote attacker can create server-side upload state, write chunk data to upload storage, trigger temporary-file processing, and cause attacker-controlled cleanup operations before authentication is enforced.

Package:

`@apostrophecms/import-export`

Confirmed affected version:

`3.6.2`

Potential earlier affected versions:

The issue may affect earlier 3.x releases in which the current big-upload-based import implementation is present. I have not yet fully verified the exact introduction version and recommend that the maintainers confirm the affected version range.

### Summary

Since 2.18.0, when an `<iframe>` is not allowed and `disallowedTagsMode` is `'discard'` (the defaults),
its raw-text content is re-sanitized by a recursive call to `sanitizeHtml(text, options)` (the change
from #5564, fixing #5550). The recursion has no bound and starts each nested call with a fresh state.
Two consequences, both absent from 2.17.7 and 2.17.4:

1. A few kilobytes of unclosed `<iframe>` tags throw `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded`
   with the default options. Any application that sanitizes untrusted HTML with 2.18.0 can be made to
   throw on a small crafted input.
2. `nestingLimit` is not enforced across a discarded iframe: each nested iframe restarts the depth
   count at zero, so the output can be nested arbitrarily deep regardless of the configured limit.

### Affected versions

- 2.18.0 (the current `latest`), and the `main` branch at the time of writing (the recursive call is
  still in `packages/sanitize-html/index.js`, in the `ontext` handler, branch
  `tag === 'iframe' && !tagAllowed(tag) && options.disallowedTagsMode === 'discard'`).
- Not affected: 2.17.7 and 2.17.4 (tested with the same inputs below).

ApostropheCMS widget styles support project-defined schema fields. If a project defines a free-form `string` style field with a CSS `property` and no selector, an editor-controlled value is rendered as an inline CSS declaration. The resulting declaration is then inserted into the widget wrapper's `style="..."` attribute without HTML-attribute escaping.

An attacker who can edit the widget can include a double quote in the style value, terminate the `style` attribute, and inject new HTML event-handler attributes. The payload is stored with the widget and executes in the Apostrophe site origin whenever the affected published page is rendered.

### Summary
ApostropheCMS lets a module expose an anonymous read API by setting `publicApiProjection`, which whitelists the document fields unauthenticated callers may see. The public REST GET handler applies every launderable query builder from the query string *before* forcing that projection. Two of those builders, `search` and `sort`, operate on the underlying documents rather than the projected output, and neither is checked against the projection. An unauthenticated attacker can therefore:

- use `?search=<word>` as a **value oracle** to confirm and locate documents by the content of a field the projection was meant to hide, and
- use `?sort[hiddenField]=1` as an **ordering oracle** to rank documents by a hidden field's value.

This is the same confidentiality-bypass class already patched for the `choices`/`counts` builders (gated by `choicesFieldAllowedByProjection`). That gate was never applied to `search` or `sort`.

When a user exports content through `@apostrophecms/import-export`, the module copies the generated archive into uploadfs at `/exports/` and returns a public URL under `/uploads/exports/`. The filename is fully deterministic: site `shortName`, document type, a `YYYYMMDDHHmmss` timestamp, and the format extension. There is no secret token.

Anyone who can guess that path can download the archive with a normal unauthenticated HTTP GET while the file is still present (10 minutes by default, longer if the site raises `importExport.export.expiration`). That is a different model from attachment URLs, which rely on hard-to-guess IDs.

Sites that disable export, store uploads on a private backend with no anonymous read, or serve `/uploads` only behind authentication are not hit by the network download step—but the predictable naming is still a design flaw for the default local/public uploadfs layout.

Import-only workflows and imports themselves are out of scope; this is specific to the export download URL.

The path traversal fix released for [GHSA-82fw-gwwq-j7x9](https://github.com/vitest-dev/vitest/security/advisories/GHSA-82fw-gwwq-j7x9) can be bypassed on Windows by using a backslash in the redirect URL pathname.

The fixed code joins an attacker-controlled URL pathname with the Vite root using `node:path/posix`, then passes that string to Vite's file allowlist check. In Vitest 5, Vite's `server.fs.deny` is not applied as intended on Vitest's dev servers. Depending on the server, files that Vite refuses to serve by default (such as `.env`, private keys and certificates, `.npmrc`, and `.git`) or Vitest's own API token file (`.vitest-secret-token`) can be read over plain HTTP by a client that can reach the server. ## Summary

The `@apostrophecms/ai-helper` package builds the URL for a server-side image fetch by resolving a storage-relative path against `req.baseUrl`. When the site does not set a global base URL (the default), `req.baseUrl` is derived from the incoming HTTP `Host` header. An authenticated editor can generate a base64 AI image (which is persisted without a stored `url`) and then send an unauthorized `PATCH` accept request with an attacker-chosen `Host` header. The server then issues an outbound `GET` to the attacker-selected origin, producing a Server-Side Request Forgery primitive that reaches hosts and ports the client cannot otherwise contact. The affected code lives in `packages/ai-helper/modules/@apostrophecms/ai-helper-image/index.js`.

## Root Cause

The image accept route trusts `req.baseUrl` as a safe origin for constructing an internal fetch target, but `req.baseUrl` is attacker-influenced whenever the site has no configured base URL. The URL builder concatenates a default local storage path (which is relative, for example `/uploads`) and resolves it against `req.baseUrl`; because the left operand is relative, the resulting origin is taken entirely from `req.baseUrl`

- `all` handler (L318–395): `getRestQuery(req).permission(false)` (L384–385) walks every page type and returns the projection including `visibility`.

`@apostrophecms/db-connect` ships an in-memory MongoDB emulation used by its SQLite, PostgreSQL, and multipostgres adapters. Its `unsetNestedField` helper walks an attacker-controlled dotted field path with no segment validation and calls `delete` on the resolved property. Because that method is shared across the whole Node process, the deletion breaks request handling for every tenant and user until the process is restarted, giving a single request a persistent denial of service.

## Summary

The client-side helper `apos.http.parseQuery()` in ApostropheCMS builds a nested object
from a URL query string without sanitizing the keys `__proto__`, `constructor`, or
`prototype`. Parsing an attacker-controlled query string therefore writes arbitrary
properties onto `Object.prototype` (client-side prototype pollution).

ApostropheCMS's admin UI calls this parser with `window.location.search` on **every
authenticated page load** (the admin context bar's `data()` initializer). Because the admin
UI is built on Vue, a polluted, enumerable property on `Object.prototype` is then picked up
by Vue's standard element-mount routine and written to the DOM as an element property,
turning the prototype pollution into DOM-based XSS in the victim's authenticated session.
The escalation gadget is a well-known, general Vue behavior; the novel,
reportable defect is the unsanitized `parseQuery` source together with the authenticated
trigger, both of which are ApostropheCMS code.

Any user who can get **any logged-in user (from the lowest-privileged `guest` role up to the highest-privileged `admin` role)** to
open a crafted URL can execute arbitrary JavaScript in that user's session.

### Summary

A rejected upload can remain in the operating system temporary directory.

### Summary
In affected versions, the experimental tasks feature (`taskStore`) did not check which session created a task. Clients sharing one `InMemoryTaskStore` could list, read and cancel each other's tasks.

Experimental tasks are deprecated. The 2026-07-28 specification replaced them with a redesigned extension. The best course of action is to stop using them.

### Am I affected?
Only if your HTTP server passes `taskStore` to `McpServer` or `Server`. If `grep -ri taskstore --exclude-dir=node_modules .` finds nothing, you are not affected.

Affected versions: `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` 1.24.0 through 1.31.0. The 2.x packages are not affected.

### Fix
Upgrade to `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` 1.32.0 or later. Each task is now tied to the session that created it, so a client that starts a new session can no longer reach its earlier tasks.

If you cannot upgrade yet, remove `taskStore`, or create one `InMemoryTaskStore` per session.

When `typographer: true` is enabled, specially crafted Markdown can cause quadratic processing time in the smartquotes rule, potentially leading to denial of service in applications processing untrusted input.

Many opening double quotes followed by unmatched closing single quotes cause repeated scans of the entire opener stack. The same issue occurs with the quote types reversed.

The default configuration (`typographer: false`) is not affected, but this option is enabled with high probability.

```js

import { performance } from 'node:perf_hooks'

const md = new MarkdownIt({ typographer: true })

for (const k of [2000, 4000, 8000, 16000, 32000]) {
  const input = '"a '.repeat(k) + "b' ".repeat(k)
  const start = performance.now()
  md.render(input)
  console.log(input.length, (performance.now() - start).toFixed(1), 'ms')
}

Result:

|input size|time|
|-|-|
|12000|18ms|
|24000|47ms|
|48000|115ms|
|96000|428ms|
|192000|1586ms|

### Patches

Fixed in **15.0.2** and **14.3.2**.

### Workarounds

Disable typography with `typographer: false`, or disable only the smartquotes rule:

```js
md.disable('smartquotes')
```

`serveStatic` decodes the request path a second time after Hono has already decoded it for routing. A crafted request can be routed as one path and served as another, so middleware mounted on a static prefix does not run for a file under that prefix.

### Details

Hono decodes the request path once before routing. `serveStatic` decoded it again before resolving the file. With a malformed percent-encoded sequence, the first decode leaves part of the path encoded, the router matches the encoded form, and the second decode resolves the real directory. The file is still resolved inside the configured root; this is not a traversal outside it.

### Impact

An unauthenticated attacker may reach static files without the middleware on their prefix running, for example an authentication check. This affects applications that mount middleware on part of the directory served by `serveStatic`. Applications that serve only public files are not affected.

During route recognition, `@angular/router` fails to validate whether an auxiliary outlet segment in the URL matches a route configured for that specific outlet name. vulnerabilities.description:
The plugin install flow in Claude Code and Claude Desktop checked out a marketplace's pinned commit SHA using `git checkout` without verifying that the resulting HEAD matched the pinned SHA. An attacker controlling a plugin's upstream repository could create a branch named identically to the pinned 40-character SHA, causing the checkout to silently resolve to the attacker's branch tip instead of the reviewed commit, resulting in attacker-controlled code being installed bypassing the pinned hash. Exploitation required a user to install a malicious plugin, pin to a safe hash, and for the plugin source to be hosted on a git host that permitted SHA-shaped branch names.

Users on standard Claude Code auto-update have received this fix already. Users performing manual updates are advised to update to the latest version.

Thank you to Or Nevo Michrowski of Air Security for reporting this issue.

### Summary

Any authenticated Leantime user - including the lowest-privilege `readonly` role - can escalate to full administrative access by calling the JSON-RPC method `leantime.rpc.api.api.createApiKeyWithProjects` with an attacker-chosen `role` value. The server creates a new account at that role with no authorization check, and the resulting credentials work as a fully interactive admin login through the ordinary web UI. ### Summary

A Qwik server in the default configuration can be crashed with one unauthenticated HTTP request. During qwik-json body parsing, `ResourceSerializer.$fill$` does `Promise.resolve(resource._resolved)`. If `_resolved` is a plain object whose `.then` is a QRL for an unregistered symbol, the async QRL rejects, the rejection is orphaned, and Node terminates the process via its default unhandled-rejection policy.

### Impact

One unauthenticated request crashes the server. Looping keeps every replica dead as long as the attacker sends requests.

## Summary

YOURLS versions ≤1.10.4 contain an unauthenticated path traversal vulnerability that allows attackers to include and execute arbitrary PHP files on the server without any credentials.

## Details

The vulnerability exists because YOURLS uses **URL sanitization functions** (`yourls_sanitize_url()`, `yourls_esc_url()`) to filter request paths, but these functions are designed to clean URLs, not filesystem paths. They preserve `/` and `.` characters, allowing `../` sequences to pass through unfiltered.

The unsanitized keyword is then directly concatenated into a filesystem path and passed to `file_exists()` and later `include()` operations, enabling path traversal attacks.

**Data Flow:**
```
HTTP Request URI (with ../)
    ↓
yourls_get_request() (no sanitization)
    ↓
yourls_sanitize_url() (preserves / and .)
    ↓
yourls_esc_url() (permits / and . via regex)
    ↓
Keyword extraction (preserves ../)
    ↓
file_exists(YOURLS_PAGEDIR . "/$keyword.php")  ← Sink
    ↓
include(YOURLS_PAGEDIR . "/$keyword.php")      ← Code Execution
```

vulnerabilities.description: Malcolm's front nginx reverse proxy defines a "Dashboards → Arkime shortcut" location using a case-insensitive regex matcher but a case-sensitive rewrite. A request whose path segment is not exact-lowercase (for example /IDDASH2ARK/...) enters the location (the matcher fires) but evades the rewrite (no redirect is issued), so nginx falls through to the location's proxy_pass to the Arkime backend. That location is the one proxied location in the shipped config that does not include the per-location authentication file, so the request reaches Arkime unauthenticated. The same location also forwards a client-supplied X-Forwarded-User header un-overwritten, and Arkime is configured to trust X-Forwarded-User as the authenticated username — so an unauthenticated network caller can reach the Arkime backend while supplying a forged, auto-provisioned identity.

vulnerabilities.description: Malcolm's nginx Lua role-based access control (RBAC) layer decides whether an authenticated user may reach a role-restricted path (e.g. /htadmin, /auth, /admin_login, /arkime/api/esadmin, NetBox, upload endpoints) by pattern-matching the raw, percent-encoded request URI. Nginx itself, however, selects which location block actually serves the request using the percent-decoded, normalized URI. Because the RBAC check never percent-decodes its input, an authenticated low-privilege user can request an admin-only path using percent-encoding (e.g. /%68tadmin.php) and have nginx route it to the restricted location while the Lua RBAC gate evaluating the un-decoded raw string finds no matching restriction and grants access.

vulnerabilities.description:
### Description

A Regular Expression Denial of Service vulnerability in the built-in AdonisJS slug route matcher may allow a remote attacker to block the Node.js event loop using a specially crafted URL.

This affects applications using `router.matchers.slug()` on a route parameter reachable by an attacker.

### Details

The regular expression used by `router.matchers.slug()` contains adjacent greedy quantifiers with overlapping character classes:

```regex
/^[^\s-_](?!.*?[-_]{2,})([a-z0-9-\\]{1,})[^\s]*[^-_\s]$/
```

When the matcher receives a long string ending with a character rejected by the final assertion, the regular expression engine must evaluate many possible ways of dividing the input between the overlapping quantifiers before determining that it does not match.

This results in quadratic execution time. Testing measured an approximate complexity of `O(n^1.98)`.

When cache interception is enabled, `@opennextjs/cloudflare` can interpret percent-encoded paths differently during middleware matching and cache lookup.

### Summary

The TinaCMS admin builds its preview `<iframe src>` from the `/~/*` hash-router splat without checking that the value stays same-origin. A fragment with a doubled slash (`#/~//attacker.example/p`) becomes the protocol-relative URL `//attacker.example/p`, so the admin frames an external site. That same unvalidated string derives `expectedOrigin`, the only trust anchor for the admin↔preview `postMessage` channel, so the attacker's frame is treated as trusted: it can submit any GraphQL operation, which the admin executes with the signed-in editor's token and posts back to the attacker's origin.

One link, opened by a logged-in editor, gives an unauthenticated remote attacker arbitrary read and write access to the site's content API as that editor.

This includes tables containing sensitive personal data, such as frontend member records and newsletter subscriber e-mail addresses.

### Vulnerability Details

In plain terms: Contao's backend is organized into modules (e.g. "News", "Members"). Every backend user is assigned to a group, and that group decides which modules, and therefore which database tables, they are allowed to work with. Before Contao lets a user touch a table, it is supposed to check: "does this user's group actually include this table?"

To avoid doing that check over and over, Contao remembers the answer for the rest of the request. The problem is that it remembers the answer under the wrong label. Instead of remembering "is this user allowed to access table X", it only remembers "is this user allowed to access something", without recording which table the answer was actually about.

Symfony resolves the class with `getReflectionClass($class, false)`, gets `null`, silently skips the interface based autoconfiguration that would have tagged it as a voter, and the now untagged private service is removed when the container is compiled. The application boots without a warning, and the ownership rule in `PreviewVoter::hasAccess()` is never executed. `tl_preview_link` has no compensating SQL filter on `createdBy`, so any non administrator back end user whose group holds the `preview_link` module reads every preview link on the installation and lifts the already signed share URLs straight out of the list. Following one grants front end preview of the target page, with `showUnpublished` and with no page permission check, to anyone at all.

### Impact

A non administrator back end user reads every preview link on the installation, including links created by administrators, and lifts the already signed share URLs out of the list. Following one grants front end previe

`RequestTokenListener` is the only generic `REQUEST_TOKEN` validator in Contao and it only runs on POST. On the GET side the guard is local and declarative, and it only fires when an `act` parameter is present. Every back end action dispatched through a different parameter therefore has no CSRF protection at all. This is a family rather than a single bug.

### Impact

An attacker who gets a logged in back end user to load a URL performs back end actions as that user, with no token and no confirmation. Because the exposure follows from the dispatch mechanism rather than from one callback, every present and future `key=` action inherits it.

**Honest bound.** The victim must be authenticated in the back end and must load the URL, and the reachable actions are limited to the modules that user can access. We have not found a `key=` action that grants privileges; the ones we verified are destructive or state changing rather than escalating.

An unauthenticated front end visitor can post a comment containing a XSS injection. The victim is any back end user who opens the Comments module, and moderation makes exposure certain rather than preventing it. No `Content-Security-Policy` header is sent on the Contao back end, so nothing mitigates the inline handler.

### Impact

Anyone on the internet can inject script that executes in the Contao back end origin, under the session of whichever user opens the Comments module, with no click and no hover. From there the payload acts as that user through the back end: reading any module they can reach, creating a new administrator, or editing a template, which on Contao is a documented path from back end write access to code execution. Moderation does not help and in fact guarantees exposure, since unpublished comments are still inserted and a moderator has to open the list to act on them.

`ImagesController` joins the user controlled `{path}` onto the configured image target directory with `Path::join()`, which canonicalises `..` segments, and never calls `Path::isBasePath()` to confirm the result stayed inside that directory. An unauthenticated GET with percent encoded dot segments therefore escapes the directory and the file is returned by `BinaryFileResponse`. Reads are bounded to the extensions in `contao.image.valid_extensions`, and paths below the upload directory fail for an unrelated reason, so this is reported as a missing boundary check rather than as a general arbitrary file read. Both Apache with the shipped `public/.htaccess` and nginx with the documented configuration are affected.

### Impact

Any unauthenticated visitor can read files that are deliberately kept outside the document root, anywhere under the project directory, as long as the name ends in one of `contao.image.valid_extensions` (`jpg`, `jpeg`, `gif`, `png`, `tif`, `tiff`, `bmp`, `svg`, `svgz`, `webp`). The route also acts as an existence oracle for arbitrary paths, and on a debug enabled instance the 404 message discloses the absolute filesystem path.

`ModuleRegistration::compile()` reaches its follow-up registration branch on **any** POST to a page carrying the module. That branch checks neither `FORM_SUBMIT` nor the captcha result computed immediately above it, and `resendActivationMail()` leads to `OptInToken::send()`, which has no rate limit at all.

### Impact

Anyone on the internet can make a Contao installation send unlimited mail to an address of their choosing, from the site's own sender and reputation, at one outbound message per HTTP request. That is both a nuisance for the recipient and a deliverability risk for the site operator. The same request is a reliable account oracle for "this address has a pending registration on this site", which is exactly the sort of membership fact a public site is usually expected not to disclose.

**Honest bound.** The target must have an unconfirmed registration, that is `tl_member.disable = 1` together with an unconfirmed `reg-` opt-in token. An attacker can create that state for an arbitrary address, since registration requires no ownership proof, but on a site where `reg_activate` is off the branch is unreachable.

`ModuleSearch` decides whether to filter protected pages out of search results based on the current value of `contao.search.index_protected`, but the authorisation data lives per row in `tl_search`. Turning the setting off removes
the filter without removing the rows, so protected pages that were indexed while it was on are returned to unauthenticated visitors such as title, URL and context snippet, even though the pages themselves still answer 401.

## Impact

Disclosure of member-only page titles, URLs and indexed text to unauthenticated visitors through the site search. The pages themselves remain access-controlled, so this is not a page-access bypass.

### Summary

`fast-jwt` 6.2.4 silently classifies raw serialized public JWK JSON
as an HMAC secret.

If an application supplies public JWK JSON text as the verifier key and
HS256 is explicitly allowed or automatically inferred, an attacker who
knows the same public JSON text can use it as an HMAC key and create an
arbitrary HS256 token that `fast-jwt` accepts as valid.

This can result in authentication or authorization bypass through forged
JWT claims.

The PoC demonstrates the issue with a serialized RSA public JWK. The same
non-PEM classification also applies to raw JWKS JSON text, although the
attached standalone PoC focuses on the smallest JWK case.

### Details

The verifier accepts a string or Buffer as key material. In
`src/crypto.js`, `performDetectPublicKeyAlgorithms()` attempts to infer
the permitted algorithm family from the supplied string.

Strings matching supported PEM public-key formats are classified as
asymmetric keys. Any other non-empty string is assumed to be an HMAC
secret:

```js
function performDetectPublicKeyAlgorithms(key) {
  const trimmedKey = key.trim()
  const publicKeyPemMatch = trimmedKey.match(publicKeyPemMatcher)

  if (trimmedKey.match(privateKey

### Summary

The fix for CVE-2026-34950 (CVSS 9.1, released in v6.2.0) is **incomplete**. It adds `key.trim()` to the PEM-detection path in `src/crypto.js`, but `String.prototype.trim()` only strips characters classified as whitespace by the ECMAScript specification. The subsequent `^`-anchored regex (`/^-----BEGIN(?: (RSA))? PUBLIC KEY-----/`) still requires the PEM header at position 0 — so **any non-whitespace leading byte** (control chars, zero-width unicode, `#` comments, HTTP-style headers, PGP wrappers) bypasses detection and falls through to the HMAC verification path, using the RSA public key as the HMAC shared secret. Net result: the **exact same RSA→HS256 algorithm-confusion attack** the original CVE addressed is fully re-enabled with a slightly different leading byte.

**Attack prerequisites are identical to CVE-2026-34950**: attacker knows the target's public RSA key (which is public by definition), and the target loads that key from a source whose content may have a non-whitespace prefix (DB column with corrupted encoding, YAML config with inline comment, copy-paste from formatted document, etc.).

**Verified on fast-jwt@6.2.2 (latest as of 2026-04-23) with a 10-line

### Summary
`cacheSet` only derives its `exp` cache deadline inside `hasIat` (`src/verifier.js:127-140`). JWT `iat` is optional. For a valid token with `exp` but no `iat`, `cacheSet` substitutes `clockTimestamp + clockTolerance + cacheTTL` (`src/verifier.js:142-146`). Later, the cache path returns the saved payload before decoding or invoking `verifyToken` (`src/verifier.js:372-388`). Since expiration validation is in `verifyToken`, the expired token remains accepted until the cache deadline.

### Details
The bug is an expiration-check bypass caused by caching.

Normally, verification works like this:

  1. Verify signature.
  2. Check exp against the current time.
  3. Return the JWT claims.

With caching enabled, `fast-jwt` saves successful verification results so it can avoid repeating crypto work for the same token.

The intended invariant is:

  > A cached token must stop being accepted at the same time as a non-cached token.

But the cache computes its expiration incorrectly.

In `fast-jwt/src/verifier.js:127`, the code first checks whether the payload has an iat (“issued at”) claim:

```js
const hasIat = payload && typeof payload.iat === 'number'

if (hasIat) {
  if (!ignore

When an application passes untrusted input to a route whose first path segment is dynamic, a value beginning with / can produce a scheme-relative URL. For example:

```ts
router.get('/:page', handler).as('pages.show')

response.redirect().toRoute('pages.show', {
  page: '/evil.example.com',
})
```

This generates the following redirect:

```http
Location: //evil.example.com
```

Browsers interpret this value as an external URL and redirect the user to `https://evil.example.com`.

The shared `createURL()` helper is used by route URL builders, including `Router.makeUrl()` and `Response.redirect().toRoute()`.

Route parameter values were appended without encoding:

```ts
if (isDefined) {

}
```

Wildcard parameters had the same behavior:

```ts
uriSegments.push(`${values.join('/')}${token.end}`)
```

**The issue does not affect APIs that intentionally accept complete redirect URLs. Exploitation requires an application to pass attacker-controlled data as a route parameter and use the generated URL as a redirect destination.**

`DsfParser.parseChunks` skips an unrecognised chunk's payload with an **un-awaited** call:
```js
this.tokenizer.ignore(Number(chunkHeader.size) - ChunkHeader.len);   // lib/dsf/DsfParser.js:51 — no await
```
`ChunkHeader.len` is 12. A crafted `.dsf` chunk with `id != 'fmt '` and `size` in `0..11` makes the

Applications generated by generator-jhipster v9.2.0 can persist user-controlled Blob ContentType values and later use those values as the MIME type for client-side Blob objects. The shared generated `openFile` helper creates an object URL from the Blob and opens it in a new window.

For Blob-bearing entities writable by normal authenticated users, this creates a stored XSS chain: attacker-controlled Blob content and MIME type are stored through the generated REST API, returned to privileged users, and opened as a same-origin Blob document from the generated Angular/React/Vue UI. Exploitability should be confirmed against the generated app’s CSP and target browsers.

## Details
The root cause is a trust-boundary failure across generated server and client code. The generated entity REST resource accepts request bodies for entity creation and update. Unless an entity-specific authority is configured, the template omits method-level `@PreAuthorize`, leaving the endpoint available to any authenticated user under the global `/api/**` security rule.

### Impact

A truncated `map32` header causes an out-of-bounds buffer read and throws `RangeError` instead of `IncompleteBufferError`. Applications that rely on `IncompleteBufferError` to wait for additional bytes may terminate a request, stream, or worker unexpectedly. No adjacent memory is disclosed because the buffer implementation checks bounds.

### Patches

The decoder now validates the complete five-byte `map32` header before reading its length and reports truncated input as `IncompleteBufferError`.

### Workarounds

Require at least five bytes before decoding a value beginning with `0xdf`, or catch `RangeError` and treat it as incomplete input only for truncated `map32` headers.

### Impact

Passing an empty or partial options object disables the default `protoAction: 'error'` protection. A map containing a `__proto__` key can then replace the prototype of the decoded object, potentially changing inherited properties or causing unexpected behavior in downstream code.

Only the decoded object's prototype is affected; this does not modify `Object.prototype` globally.

### Patches

Options are now merged with secure defaults without modifying the caller's object. Unsupported `protoAction` values are rejected.

### Workarounds

Explicitly set `protoAction: 'error'` whenever constructing a msgpack5 instance, and validate decoded values before use.

### Impact

The streaming decoder recursively invokes itself for every complete value remaining in a chunk. A single chunk containing many small valid MessagePack values can exhaust the JavaScript call stack and interrupt the process or stream.

### Patches

The streaming decoder now drains concatenated values iteratively with constant call-stack depth.

### Workarounds

Limit the number of MessagePack values accepted in one chunk, or split large batches before passing them to the decoder stream.

### Impact

The reserved MessagePack byte `0xc1` is incorrectly treated as incomplete input. When it appears at the start of a decoder stream, all subsequent data is retained while the decoder waits for bytes that can never make the value valid, allowing memory exhaustion.

### Patches

The decoder now rejects `0xc1` as invalid input. Streaming decoders release buffered input and stop after unrecoverable decoding errors.

### Workarounds

Reject `0xc1` before streaming input to msgpack5, and enforce stream byte and time limits.

### Impact

The decoder has no nesting-depth limit for arrays and maps. An attacker who can provide MessagePack input can use deeply nested containers to exhaust the JavaScript call stack and interrupt the process or request handler.

### Patches

The decoder now limits nesting depth to 100 by default and throws `Maximum decode depth exceeded`. Applications can configure the limit with the `maxDepth` option.

### Workarounds

Reject deeply nested input before decoding, isolate decoding in a worker, or enforce a trusted schema with a bounded nesting depth.

vulnerabilities.description:
### Summary

The MediaBundle blocks dangerous upload extensions with a blacklist that was matched
case-sensitively, while the stored filename was lowercased afterwards. A file uploaded
as `webshell.pHp` therefore bypassed the blacklist and was written to the web-accessible
upload directory as `webshell.php`, where the web server executed it. Any authenticated
backend user with access to the media section could obtain remote code execution.

### Details

`FileHandler::getFilePath()` rewrote blacklisted extensions to `.txt` using a
case-sensitive regex, and only then lowercased the extension when building the stored
name — so the check ran against the attacker-controlled casing and the normalisation
happened after it.

Two further weaknesses contributed:

* The default blacklist contained only `php` and `htaccess`, leaving other
  server-executable extensions (`phtml`, `php5`, `phar`, `shtml`, `cgi`, …) unblocked
  regardless of casing.
* Configured blacklist values were interpolated into the regex unescaped.

vulnerabilities.description:
### Impact
Improper neutralization of special elements in data query logic in the GridFS component of the MongoDB PHP Library can cause a caller-supplied structured file identifier to be interpreted as a query condition rather than as a literal identifier. An authenticated user who can influence the identifier passed by an affected application may obtain stored file content beyond the intended target or cause all GridFS file chunks in the affected bucket to be removed, rendering stored file content unreadable. The affected rename operation may also rename a stored file other than the intended target.


### Patches
Fixed in 1.21.5 and 2.4.2.

### Workarounds
Validate GridFS IDs.

### References
https://jira.mongodb.org/browse/PHPLIB-1929

vulnerabilities.description:
App-based multi-factor authentication management actions did not consistently require the user to confirm their current password. In particular, an authenticated session could set up app-based MFA and obtain recovery codes without password reauthentication. Disabling app-based MFA and regenerating recovery codes also accepted an existing app code or recovery code without requiring the current password. This issue does not affect email-based MFA.

If an attacker gains access to a user's authenticated session, they could enable app-based MFA and obtain recovery codes without knowing the user's password, changing the account's MFA configuration and potentially locking the legitimate user out. This issue does not by itself allow an unauthenticated attacker to sign in.

vulnerabilities.description: RT-Labs AB C-Open CANopen contains a write protection bypass in the SDO (Service Data Object) server implementation 'src/co_sdo_server.c' that fails to properly validate write permissions when processing download-segment frames. An unauthenticated attacker on the CAN bus can initiate an SDO upload for a read-only Object Dictionary (OD) entry, which sets a data pointer to the read-only object, then send download-segment frames to write to that memory location. The download-segment handler does not verify that a download session is active, allowing any CANopen node to overwrite read-only OD entries using two SDO frames. Note that CANopen protocol operates over CAN bus and does not provide built-in authentication mechanisms. Fixed in 1.1.1.
vulnerabilities.action: Fixed in 1.1.1.

vulnerabilities.description: Johnson Controls is aware of a vulnerability in EasyIO Neo which may allow an attacker to intercept and read sensitive information, including credentials and session data, transmitted in cleartext over the network. vulnerabilities.action: If immediate update is not possible, Johnson Controls recommends the following mitigations: Enable and enforce HTTPS/TLS for all web-based management access to the device. ### Impact

PHPCSUtils versions 1.0.0-alpha1 through 1.2.2 contain an arbitrary code execution vulnerability in `PHPCSUtils\AbstractSniffs\AbstractArrayDeclarationSniff::getActualArrayKey()`. The vulnerable method is reached by any sniff that extends `AbstractArrayDeclarationSniff` and calls `getActualArrayKey()`.

Running PHPCS over untrusted PHP code through such a sniff, for example, in a CI pipeline that lints pull requests, or on a developer machine reviewing third-party code, could lead to arbitrary command execution on the scanning host.

The vulnerability happens when the method determines the value of an array key using `eval()`. A maliciously crafted array key such as `'system'('id')` would be executed when the code was scanned.

### Known attack vectors

Known code paths that reach the vulnerable method include the following PHPCSExtra sniffs:

- `Universal.Arrays.DuplicateArrayKey`
- `Universal.Arrays.MixedArrayKeyTypes`

Other packages that call `AbstractArrayDeclarationSniff::getActualArrayKey()` may also be vulnerable.

### Patches

This issue has been fixed in PHPCSUtils 1.2.3. We recommend all users upgrade to 1.2.3 or later.

vulnerabilities.description:
### Impact

An unauthenticated account takeover vulnerability exists in `fof/oauth` when the Discord OAuth provider is enabled.

Discord allows an account to use an unverified email address when its phone number has been verified. During OAuth authentication, Discord may return that email address with `"verified": false`.

Affected versions of `fof/oauth` did not validate this flag and passed the email address to Flarum core as trusted via `provideTrustedEmail()`. Flarum core could then match the trusted email address to an existing user, link the attacker-controlled Discord identity to that user, and authenticate the attacker as the victim.

An attacker who knows a user's email address can therefore take over the corresponding Flarum account without knowing its password or requiring any interaction from the victim. This includes administrator accounts.

#### Preconditions for exploitation

1. Discord sign-in is enabled on the forum.
2. The victim has a Flarum account with a known email address.
3. The victim's email address is not already associated with a Discord account.
4. The attacker creates or configures a Discord account using the victim's email address without verifying it

vulnerabilities.description:
### Impact
The vulnerability allows an attacker to bypass the HTML sanitizer by using the `data-html-content` attribute in the content of a `SharpEditorFormField`. 

### Patches
The field must now explicitly configure `SharpFormEditorField::RAW_HTML` in the toolbar to keep this behavior. **When using the  `RAW_HTML` button, the application using `code16/sharp` must sanitize manually the content coming from the field**. 
Vulnerability has been patched in version 9.22.5.

### Workarounds
Sanitize every contents of editors manually (e.g. using Symfony/HtmlSanitizer)

### Impact
A Stored Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability exists in the rich text editor due to improper sanitization of the srcdoc attribute on <iframe> elements.

While the underlying Symfony HtmlSanitizer correctly HTML-encodes special characters inside the attribute value (e.g., converting <script> to <script>), the HTML specification mandates that browsers automatically decode HTML entities inside attribute values before processing them. As a result, any encoded JavaScript inside a srcdoc attribute is evaluated and executed as live HTML/JS in the context of the iframe when the page is rendered.

An attacker with permissions to edit an Editor field can inject malicious scripts to target other users viewing the content. Potential impacts include:

- Session Hijacking (stealing admin session cookies via document.cookie)
- Account Takeover & Privilege Escalation (e.g., a low-privileged editor triggering actions as an Administrator)
- Admin panel data theft

### Patches
The vulnerability has been patched in version v9.22.5.

The fix explicitly removes srcdoc from the list of allowed iframe attributes in `src/Utils/Sanitization/FormatsSanitizedValue.php`.

### Workarounds
U

### Summary
With $wgEmbedVideoRequireConsent disabled (not the default), the urls for videos are passed into an iframe src attribute without sanitization. When given a malformed url or id, the src attribute can be escaped via double quotes, allowing for html/javascript injection.

### Details
The iframe assembled [here](https://github.com/StarCitizenWiki/mediawiki-extensions-EmbedVideo/blob/a573a16d925ee0ea0d34b360856dc8ab0b88f822/includes/EmbedService/EmbedHtmlFormatter.php#L204-L208) adds the url from `getUrl()` as the src without sanitization.
The id regex for the archiveorg service and the url regexes for the wistia and sharepoint services allow for double quotes to be introduced.

### PoC
Using double quotes, the src attribute can be escaped.
```
<embedvideo service="archiveorg" id='a" onmouseover="alert(document.domain)" data-x="'></embedvideo>
```

### Impact
When $wgEmbedVideoRequireConsent = false, any user able to edit a page can inject arbitrary JavaScript into an HTML event handler attribute (e.g. onfocus) via parameter. It requires no interaction (autofires via autofocus) and executes in the wiki origin for every visitor to the page.

vulnerabilities.description:
Snipe-IT's uploaded-files API accepts XML documents and later serves them inline without applying the safe-inline allowlist used by the equivalent web controller. An authenticated user who can attach files to a supported object can upload an XSLT stylesheet and an XML document that references it through xml-stylesheet. When another authorized user opens the XML file through the API with ?inline=true, the browser applies the attacker-controlled stylesheet, which produces HTML containing JavaScript in the Snipe-IT origin.
This was reproduced against commit df8e3b144331d0c1cc14778f900e7646d1d9a509 (v8.6.3-231-gdf8e3b1443).

The attack requires an authenticated account with file access to at least one supported object and one victim interaction. Scope changes because attacker-controlled code executes in another user's Snipe-IT security context. The script can read same-origin data available to the victim and perform authenticated actions as that victim.

### Affected Components

- app/Http/Requests/UploadFileRequest.php
Allows xml uploads through filesystems.allowed_upload_extensions_for_validator.
Sanitizes only files detected as image/svg+xml. Both files in this proof of concept are

### Impact

An attacker who knows a victim's password fully bypasses that account's 2FA and obtains a persistent token with full API access as the user (read and write across the user's permissions, including admin if the victim is an admin).

The token is an API credential, not a web/UI session (using it on web routes redirects to `/login`), but the REST API covers essentially the whole application. If the victim is an admin, the token can also call the admin `users/two_factor_reset` endpoint, which is in the same un-gated API surface, to clear the account's enrolled 2FA. The next login is then forced to re-enroll a second factor, which the password-holding attacker can complete with their own device, taking over the account's web access and locking the legitimate user out.

### Summary:

2FA is enforced only by the `web` middleware group, not the `api` group, and the personal-access-token endpoint is in the `api` group. A session that has passed the password check but not the 2FA can mint a persistent API token and use it for full API access. 


### Details:

### Impact

An uncontrolled resource consumption / algorithmic complexity vulnerability affecting any application that parses untrusted email with this library.

Three independent parsing paths are super-linear in cost, so a byte-size cap on the caller side does **not** bound the work done.  A crafted message under 2 MB can consume seconds of CPU or hundreds of megabytes to multiple gigabytes of memory (leading to an out-of-memory kill), enabling denial of service. The parse is lazy, but the cost is paid on the first `getAllParts()` or content read.

### Details

1. **Deep multipart nesting is O(depth²).** `MimeParserService::findContentBoundary()` tests each content line against the current part and every ancestor via the recursive `ParserMimePartProxy::setEndBoundaryFound()`, so a nesting depth of D costs 1 + 2 + … + D comparisons. A ~600 KB message nested ~10,000 deep does not finish parsing in a minute.
2. **Many sibling parts is O(n²).** `PartChildrenContainer::add()` appends each child with `array_splice($children, count($children), 0, [$part])`, which reindexes the entire array on every call. The same container backs UUEncoded `begin` parts via `NonMimeParserService`.

### Impact

A CRLF (carriage-return / line-feed) header injection  affecting any application that uses this library to build or forward MIME messages with an attacker-influenced attachment filename.
  
Attachment filenames are interpolated into the `Content-Type` and `Content-Disposition` header values without stripping CR/LF, so a filename containing `\r\n` serializes as one or more additional, attacker-controlled header lines (for example a forged `Bcc:` that silently exfiltrates a copy of the outgoing message). The untrusted filename can come directly from parsed inbound mail, so no local construction is required — an application that re-attaches or re-sends a parsed filename is exposed.

### Details

On the outbound side, `MultipartHelper::createAndAddPartForAttachment()` sanitizes the filename only with `iconv('UTF-8','US-ASCII//translit//ignore', $filename)`. CR and LF are valid US-ASCII, so they survive that filter, and the value is then written into the header verbatim via `MimePart::setRawHeader()`. A filename of `doc\r\nBcc: attacker@evil.test` therefore serializes as:

```
Content-Disposition: attachment;
 filename="doc
Bcc: attacker@evil.test"
```

vulnerabilities.description: Plex Media Server before 1.43.3.10861 builds a file path from the url parameter without checking it for ../ sequences, allowing path traversal via '/system/agents/media/get'. A remote attacker with a valid session token could read any file that the target user can access. This access includes the PlexOnlineToken, which grants control of the Plex account and server. A LAN-adjacent attacker with a client-supplied X-Forwarded-For header could exploit the same issue.

### Impact

An unauthenticated JCR-SQL2 injection exists in the Smart Content category filter of the 2.x content query builder.

Category IDs supplied through the public `?categories=` query parameter are only trimmed and are then concatenated directly into a JCR-SQL2 `WHERE` clause, without the numeric validation that the equivalent tag filter already performs. Any public page that renders a Smart Content element with category filtering enabled evaluates this parameter, so no authentication or special configuration beyond a category-filtered content block is required.

An anonymous visitor can therefore:

- inject boolean conditions to infer the existence of, and disclose, content nodes they should not see (for example unpublished pages) via blind boolean-based extraction; and
- submit malformed query fragments that cause query errors or resource-intensive queries, degrading availability.

Because the sink is a JCR-SQL2 query, the impact is limited to reading and enumerating content-repository nodes and to error/denial-of-service conditions; it cannot be used to modify data through this path.

### Patches

Fixed in **2.6.25 and 3.0.8**. Category, tag, and audience-target-group IDs

## Summary

WPGraphQL 2.19.0 contains an authorization bypass in the `updatePost` mutation. An authenticated WordPress Contributor can change one of their own draft posts to `PUBLISH` despite lacking the `publish_posts` capability. The same mutation also permits the Contributor to modify their own previously published posts despite lacking `edit_published_posts` and failing WordPress's object-level `edit_post` capability check.

This bypasses the standard WordPress editorial workflow. The WordPress REST API correctly rejects the equivalent operations for the same user.

## Affected software

- Plugin: WPGraphQL
- Plugin slug: `wp-graphql`
- Confirmed affected version: `2.19.0`
- Plugin URL: https://wordpress.org/plugins/wp-graphql/
- Repository: https://github.com/wp-graphql/wp-graphql
- WordPress version used for testing: `7.0.2`
- WPGraphQL configuration: default settings

Only version 2.19.0 is claimed as confirmed because that is the version tested. The same authorization pattern appears in earlier source history, but those releases were not independently tested.

## Vulnerability type

- Broken access control / authorization bypass
- CWE-863: Incorrect Authorization
- OWASP 20

### Impact

The control panel action `formie/sent-notifications/get-resend-modal-content` (`SentNotificationsController::actionGetResendModalContent`) performed only `requireAcceptsJson()` and loaded a `SentNotification` by request `id` without permission or object-level authorization checks.

Any authenticated user who could invoke the action could enumerate notification IDs and read full email content — including recipient headers and the complete HTML body containing submitted form data (PII) — without `formie-accessSentNotifications` or equivalent permission. Sibling actions in the same controller enforced authorization.

### Patches

Fixed in **3.1.31** (Craft 5) and **2.2.23** (Craft 4).

Craft 5: `canView()` is enforced after loading, consistent with `actionEdit`.  
Craft 4: `formie-viewSentNotifications` permission is required.

### Workarounds

Restrict CP access to trusted users only until upgraded. No configuration workaround.

- Reported by Jorge González (jorge@jmilla.es)

### Impact

The anonymous front-end action `formie/submissions/submit` (`SubmissionsController::actionSubmit`) trusted a client-supplied `submissionId` when loading an incomplete submission, with no session binding, ownership check, or edit token validation.

An unauthenticated attacker could enumerate sequential submission IDs and overwrite or hijack another user's in-progress (multi-page / save-for-later) submission. Tampered data could be persisted and forwarded via notifications and integrations when the submission was completed.

Completed submissions were not affected (`isIncomplete=true` filter). This is an incomplete remediation of [GHSA-pgxq-p76c-x9cg](https://github.com/advisories?query=GHSA-pgxq-p76c-x9cg), which added edit-token validation to `save-submission` but not to `submit`.

### Patches

Fixed in **3.1.31** (Craft 5) and **2.2.23** (Craft 4).

When resuming an existing submission on a site request, the submission ID must match the session-bound submission (`Form::getCurrentSubmission()`) or a valid `submissionEditToken` when `editingSubmission` is set. Cross-form submission ID reuse is also rejected.

### Impact

The control panel action `formie/integrations/form-settings` (`IntegrationsController::actionFormSettings`) was reachable by any authenticated user without the appropriate form integration permissions. The action applied request-supplied settings to a fully configured integration via `setAttributes($settings, false)`, allowing an attacker to overwrite outbound host properties (e.g. `apiUrl`) while the server sent stored API keys or OAuth tokens to the attacker-controlled host. The remote response was returned in the JSON body (non-blind SSRF).

This is an incomplete remediation of [GHSA-cvpc-hccg-wmw4](https://github.com/advisories?query=GHSA-cvpc-hccg-wmw4). The `form-settings` action was excluded from the permission gate added in 3.1.28.

### Summary

A limited server-side Twig template injection issue was identified in Solspace Freeform for Craft CMS. In affected versions, submitted form field values could be evaluated as Twig in certain rendering contexts.

Unauthenticated users could submit Twig expressions through public Freeform forms and have those expressions evaluated when the submitted values were rendered back into the form response. Confirmed impact includes disclosure of limited server/environment information, such as the PHP version and absolute filesystem paths.

No evidence was found that this issue allowed access to Craft globals, environment variables, database credentials, mailer credentials, security keys, or remote code execution in the tested environment.

### Details

**Plugin:** Solspace Freeform
**Affected versions:** Freeform 5.0.0 through 5.10.13
**CMS:** Craft CMS
**Authentication required:** None
**Attack vector:** Public Freeform form submission

Submitted field values were passed through Freeform’s isolated Twig renderer. As a result, Twig expressions included in submitted values could be evaluated server-side and reflected in the HTTP response.

When an administrator attempts to delete a media file that is referenced by a Media Manager effect, the warning message rendered in the backend includes the type's `name` field without HTML escaping. vulnerabilities.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

openvswitch: vport: fix self-deadlock on release of tunnel ports

vports are used concurrently and protected by RCU, so netdev_put()
must happen after the RCU grace period.  So, either in an RCU call or
after the synchronize_net().  The rtnl_delete_link() must happen under
RTNL and so can't be executed in RCU context.  Calling synchronize_net()
while holding RTNL is not a good idea for performance and system
stability under load in general, so calling netdev_put() in RCU call
is the right solution here.

However,
when the device is deleted, rtnl_unlock() will call netdev_run_todo()
and block until all the references are gone.  In the current code this
means that we never reach the call_rcu() and the vport is never freed
and the reference is never released, causing a self-deadlock on device
removal.

Fix that by moving the rcu_call() before the rtnl_unlock(), so the
scheduled RCU callback will be executed when synchronize_net() is
called from the rtnl_unlock()->netdev_run_todo() while the RTNL itself
is already released.

In order to apply a particular protection key to an address range, the kernel must update the corresponding page table entries.  The subroutine which handled this failed to take into account the presence of 1GB largepage mappings created using the shm_create_largepage(3) interface. In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

Bluetooth: btintel: serialize btintel_hw_error() with hci_req_sync_lock

btintel_hw_error() issues two __hci_cmd_sync() calls (HCI_OP_RESET
and Intel exception-info retrieval) without holding
hci_req_sync_lock().  This lets it race against
hci_dev_do_close() -> btintel_shutdown_combined(), which also runs
__hci_cmd_sync() under the same lock.  When both paths manipulate
hdev->req_status/req_rsp concurrently, the close path may free the
response skb first, and the still-running hw_error path hits a
slab-use-after-free in kfree_skb().

is serialized with every other synchronous HCI command issuer.

vulnerabilities.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

Bluetooth: L2CAP: Fix deadlock in l2cap_conn_del()

l2cap_conn_del() calls cancel_delayed_work_sync() for both info_timer
and id_addr_timer while holding conn->lock. However, the work functions
l2cap_info_timeout() and l2cap_conn_update_id_addr() both acquire
conn->lock, creating a potential AB-BA deadlock if the work is already
executing when l2cap_conn_del() takes the lock.

Move the work cancellations before acquiring conn->lock and use
disable_delayed_work_sync() to additionally prevent the works from
being rearmed after cancellation, consistent with the pattern used in
hci_conn_del().

vulnerabilities.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

Bluetooth: btusb: clamp SCO altsetting table indices

btusb_work() maps the number of active SCO links to USB alternate
settings through a three-entry lookup table when CVSD traffic uses
transparent voice settings. The lookup currently indexes alts[] with
data->sco_num - 1 without first constraining sco_num to the number of
available table entries.

While the table only defines alternate settings for up to three SCO
links, data->sco_num comes from hci_conn_num() and is used directly.
Cap the lookup to the last table entry before indexing it so the
driver keeps selecting the highest supported alternate setting without
reading past alts[].
